---
title: "Oversampling"
description: "A data-balancing technique that increases the representation of underrepresented classes in a training dataset."
term: "Oversampling"
letter: "O"
category: "Data Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Oversampling gives a minority class more presence during training. It can
do this by repeating examples or generating additional synthetic examples,
so a model has more opportunity to learn from that class.

## Technical explanation

Random oversampling duplicates minority-class examples. Synthetic
oversampling methods such as SMOTE create new feature vectors by
interpolating among minority examples. These approaches change the
effective training distribution and can affect both decision boundaries
and probability calibration.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Imbalanced labels can make a model favor the majority class, even when
minority cases are important. Oversampling is one option alongside
class-weighted losses, data collection, and threshold adjustment. The
choice should reflect the task's error costs and evaluation metrics.

## How it works

For random oversampling, select minority examples with replacement until
the desired class balance is reached. For synthetic approaches, create
examples using local relationships in feature space. Apply resampling only
to training data and within each training fold to avoid leakage.

## Practical example

In fraud detection, a training set may contain far fewer fraud cases than
legitimate transactions. Oversampling can increase minority examples
during training, while final evaluation should use a held-out set that
reflects the deployment distribution.

## Common misconceptions

- Oversampling does not add genuinely new information when it simply duplicates examples.
- A balanced training set does not mean production class frequencies are balanced.
- Resampling before a train/test split can leak information and produce misleading evaluation.
